relations.note: Huallallo opposes or kills the young Amaru in the romance cycle.
Huallallo releases Amaru as a weapon against Pariacaca.
Huallallo releases the two-headed monster against Pariacaca, who strikes and petrifies it.
Some modern Junín versions identify Amaru as Pariacaca's son.
Amaru confronts Pariacaca, who pierces its back with a golden staff.
Pariacaca's golden staff makes Amaru grow cold and become stone.
Viracocha orders Tulumanya to engender Amaru during a catastrophe.
Cuniraya places semen in a lucuma fruit that Cavillaca unknowingly eats.
After learning his paternity, Cavillaca flees Cuniraya and becomes stone at the sea.
Pariacaca and Cuniraya occupy overlapping cultic and narrative spheres without a harmonized genealogy.
Pariacaca overwhelms the fiery Huanca patron with storm, flood, snow, and cold.
Mountain powers overlap with Illapa through thunder, lightning, hail, rain, and summit sacrifice.
Inca ceremonies offered to both solar and mountain powers without establishing universal kinship.
Apus and Pachamama are jointly addressed in offerings, while their precise kinship varies regionally.
Illimani and other ancestral mountains are honored jointly with Pachamama in Bolivian rites.
Tío or Supay may be understood as an underground aspect or transformed form of mountain ownership.
Manco Cápac is presented as the Sun’s child or emissary.
Mama Huaco is paired with Ayar Cachi in Sarmiento’s allocation.
A variant gives Mama Huaco to Manco after Cachi’s removal.
Mama Huaco belongs to the eightfold sibling founding group.
Ayar Manco marries his sister Mama Ocllo.
Mama Ocllo belongs to the eightfold sibling founding group.
Viracocha creates the Ayars and commands them to emerge and rule.
relations.source: Sarmiento, Historia de los Incas, ch. 11

relations.note: Later writers functionally equate their sling-wielding lightning powers; no primary encounter exists.
Llocllayhuancupa, whom Catequil enables to speak, claims descent or commission from Pachacamac.
A disputed reading makes the Sun Chasca’s father.
Chasca attends Inti as his page, appearing before or behind him.
relations.source: Garcilaso, Comentarios reales II.21 and III.21

relations.note: Chasca’s disappearance in the Sun’s presence marks the fast’s conclusion.
relations.source: Anonymous Jesuit, Relación de las costumbres antiguas

relations.note: Chasca is positioned beneath or near the Sun in the diagram.
relations.source: Santa Cruz Pachacuti, Relación de antigüedades

relations.note: Inti and Chasca share celestial temple and calendrical classifications.
A disputed reading makes the Moon Chasca’s mother.
Mama Quilla and Chasca appear together in the cultic hierarchy and festival list.
Cuniraya secretly places semen in a lúcuma fruit, which Cahuillaca eats unknowingly.
After their child identifies Cuniraya, he pursues Cahuillaca until she enters the sea.
While Pachacamac is absent, Cuniraya assaults his daughters and damages Urpayhuachac’s fish pond.
The text reports that Cuniraya created Pariacaca.
People consequently call Cuniraya Pariacaca's father.
Cuniraya secretly impregnates Cahuillaca through a lúcuma fruit.
The compound Cuniraya Viracocha fuses the local huaca with Viracocha's name and creator functions.
Modern scholarship extends a Tunupa–Viracocha equation to Ekeko without primary narrative evidence.
Pariacaca overwhelms Huallallo's immense fire with rain, hail, lightning, cold, and flood.
Pariacaca defeats Huallallo with storms and floods, driving him toward the Antis.
Pariacaca sentences the defeated human-eater to eat dogs and receive Huanca worship.

relations.myth: Seven huacas confronted by Pachacuti Inca
relations.note: Huallallo and Pariacaca jointly appear among seven curaca-like huacas subordinated by Pachacuti Inca.
Garcilaso interprets Illapa’s lightning, thunder, and bolt as servants of Inti.
Illapa stands below or beside Inti in offerings and state ritual.
Inti and Illapa receive coordinated offerings within state ritual.
The regional Sullca Illapa is listed among Pariacaca’s sons.
Illapa’s image accompanies the Maker in processions, offerings, and cult rankings.
Some unstable regional traditions present Kon as Inti's offspring.
relations.source: Lope de Gómara and later compilations

relations.myth: Dowry before marriage to Manco Cápac
relations.note: Mama Huaco requests a marriage dowry from the Sun, who supplies it.
Guamán Poma uniquely identifies Mama Huaco as the Sun's daughter.
Maize associated with Mama Huaco also participates in state ceremonies serving the Sun.

relations.myth: Children of the Sun and the golden rod
relations.note: The Sun gives the founding pair a golden rod to locate Cusco.

relations.myth: The Sun sends Manco Cápac and Mama Ocllo
relations.note: Inti fathers Mama Ocllo and sends her to teach women.
Mama Ocllo and Manco Cápac are children of the Sun.

relations.myth: Children of the Sun and the golden rod
relations.note: The Sun sends Mama Ocllo to instruct humanity and establish solar rule.
The Moon is described as Inti's wife in imperial cult structure.

relations.myth: Rival brightness of Moon and Sun
relations.note: The Moon was initially brighter than the jealous Sun.
Her silver hall stood beside Inti’s principal golden chapel.
The Moon is commonly described as Inti's sister.
An unsupported modern tale says Inti transformed the maiden Sara into maize.

relations.myth: The golden staff determines Cusco's foundation
relations.note: Inti gives Manco a golden staff to locate his destined center.

relations.myth: The Sun gives the founders a golden rod
relations.note: The Sun gives Manco and Mama Ocllo a rod locating Cusco.

relations.myth: The Sun sends Manco Cápac and Mama Ocllo
relations.note: Inti fathers Manco Cápac and sends him to establish Inca order.
Manco and Mama Ocllo are presented as children of the Sun.

relations.myth: Manco prays before founding Cusco and Coricancha
relations.note: Manco prays to the Sun and establishes solar worship at Cusco.
relations.source: Cieza, El señorío de los incas

relations.myth: The starving woman and food plants
relations.note: The Sun impregnates the woman after Pachacamac fails her, provoking Pachacamac’s jealous retaliation.
Pachacamac resents solar worship, murders Inti's child, then flees Vichama.
Later Inca-colonial theology sometimes presents Pachacamac and the Sun as brothers.
Inti and Pachamama receive offerings within the same ritual field.

relations.myth: Sun and Earth as father and mother
relations.note: Inti and Pachamama appear together as paternal and maternal powers.
relations.source: Zárate, Historia del descubrimiento y conquista del Perú

relations.note: Sun and Earth are invoked together among powers protecting the Inca.

relations.myth: Creation of the Sun at Titicaca
relations.note: Viracocha creates or stations Inti and commands his cosmic course.

relations.myth: Creation of celestial light at Tiwanaku
relations.note: Viracocha creates the Sun and sets its course.
relations.source: Betanzos, Suma y narración de los Incas

relations.note: Pachacamac arrives from the south, defeats or expels Con, and replaces his creation.
Pachacamac overcomes, displaces, or drives away the earlier coastal creator Con.
Some modern retellings call Pachacamac Con’s son; early sources do not establish this.
Cuniraya enters Pachacamac’s coastal household while its absent lord never confronts him directly.
Some Huarochirí narrators uncertainly call Pariacaca a son of Cuniraya.
Cuniraya bears Viracocha as a compound name or title; its mechanism remains uncertain.

relations.myth: Terrestrial and marine fields in the Coricancha cosmogram
relations.note: Pachamama and Mama Cocha occupy corresponding terrestrial and marine positions.

relations.myth: Catalogue of worshipped earth and sea powers
relations.note: Acosta lists Pachamama and Mamacocha successively as worshipped natural powers.
relations.source: Acosta, Historia natural y moral V.4

relations.note: Garcilaso's name Mama Ocllo Huaco partly conflates the two female founders.
They migrate in the same founding company; Mama Huaco leads armed conquest.
Mama Ocllo is Mama Huaco's sister and fellow female Ayar founder.
Zuidema connects Mama Sara's seed vessel and rites with Mama Huaco's agricultural identity.
Mama Huaco and Manco Cápac jointly command the founders' migration and conquest.

relations.myth: Mama Huaco helps seize the Cusco valley
relations.note: She defeats or terrifies the Huallas and helps Manco's migrants seize Cusco.
Murúa and Guamán Poma make Mama Huaco the wife or coya of Manco Cápac.
Guamán Poma uniquely makes Mama Huaco both Manco Cápac's mother and wife.
Sarmiento and the ritual tradition make her Manco Cápac's sister.
Viracocha produces Mama Huaco and the other Ayars to become rulers.
Mama Ocllo and Manco Cápac are children of the Moon.
She is Mama Quilla’s dynastic descendant or child in later synthesis.

relations.myth: Solar couple travels from Titicaca and founds Cusco
relations.note: She co-founds Cusco, gathers women, and teaches household and textile work.
Mama Ocllo is paired as Ayar Manco's wife.
relations.source: Betanzos, Suma y narración, Part I, chapter 3

relations.myth: The Ayar migration from Tampu Tocco
relations.note: They migrate together, and Manco establishes the ruling line at Cusco.
relations.source: Betanzos, Suma y narración, Part I, chapter 3

relations.myth: Children of the Sun and the golden rod
relations.note: They travel from Titicaca, gather inhabitants, and establish Cusco together.
Mama Ocllo is Manco Cápac's legitimate sister-wife.

relations.myth: Creation of the primordial sibling collective
relations.note: Viracocha creates or commissions the founding siblings, including Mama Ocllo.
He is her dynastic descendant or child; direct maternity varies.
The Creator made or commanded the Moon to rise into heaven.
Some recent practices use Mama Sara objects as offerings to Pachamama.

relations.myth: Pachamamaachi and the roots of the Incas
relations.note: Pachamamaachi is his mother, though identification with cosmic Pachamama is disputed.

relations.myth: Creator moves the ancestors underground toward Pacaritambo
relations.note: A late variant makes the Creator bring Manco's ancestral group from Titicaca.

relations.myth: Manco founds Cusco invoking Ticci Viracocha
relations.note: Manco founds Cusco in the name of Ticci Viracocha and other gods.
relations.source: Cieza, El señorío de los incas

relations.note: Pariacaca and Pachacamac attend or are represented at the Inca's assembly of powerful huacas.
Colonial theological syntheses equate both as the supreme maker, though other evidence distinguishes them.
Cuniraya enters Pachacamac's coastal domain and household while pursuing Cahuillaca.
Some mining accounts describe Pachamama and Tío or Supay as spouses, but this is not universal.
Mine rites may address both beings as complementary or distinct recipients of offerings.
Viracocha and mama pacha occupy the same ordered cosmos without genealogy.

Anchanchu.note: This Aymara dangerous place-being is sometimes equated with the Devil or Supay-like mine spirits.

Apotampo.note: Apo Manco Cápac is named as a child of Apotampo.
Apotampo.source: Santa Cruz Pachacuti, Relación de antigüedades

Apotampo.note: Pachamamaachi is Apotampo's partner; her identification with Pachamama is uncertain.

Ataguju.note: Ataguju is Catequil’s grandfather and supreme sky-associated progenitor.

Ataguju.myth: Bringing the Huamachucos from Cerro Guacat
Ataguju.note: Catequil requests humans; Ataguju directs him to bring them from Guacat.

Axomama.note: This potato power participates with Pachamama in the agricultural generative field.

Ayar Auca.note: Ayar Auca is Mama Huaco's brother and fellow migrant in the Ayar cycle.
Some genealogical arrangements pair Mama Huaco with Ayar Auca.
Ayar Auca belongs to the same primordial sibling collective.
They belong to the founding migration; no discrete interaction is recorded.
Ayar Auca is one of Ayar Manco's three brothers.
Ayar Auca.source: Betanzos, Suma y narración de los incas

Ayar Auca.myth: Ayar Auca supernaturally takes possession of Cusco
Ayar Auca.note: Manco directs or accompanies Auca, then inherits the political result of his land-taking.

Ayar Cachi.note: Ayar Cachi is one of Mama Huaco's male Ayar siblings.
Some unstable arrangements pair Mama Huaco as Ayar Cachi's sister-wife.
Mama Huaco shames or persuades him to return to the cave, enabling his confinement.
Ayar Cachi belongs to the same primordial sibling collective.
They belong to the founding migration; no individual interaction is recorded.
Ayar Cachi is one of Ayar Manco's three brothers.
Ayar Cachi.source: Betanzos, Suma y narración de los incas

Ayar Cachi.myth: Ayar Cachi is trapped inside the origin cave
Ayar Cachi.note: Manco participates in or benefits from deceiving and enclosing his dangerous brother.

Ayar Uchu.note: Ayar Uchu belongs to the sibling founder group with Mama Huaco.
Betanzos associates her with the Ayar who disappears into the sacred landscape.
Ayar Uchu belongs to the same primordial sibling collective.
They belong to the founding migration; no discrete interaction is recorded.
Ayar Uchu is Manco's brother and becomes the Huanacauri huaca.

Ayar Uchu.myth: Ayar Uchu becomes Huanacauri and guides Manco
Ayar Uchu.note: After transformation, Ayar Uchu instructs Manco and promises continued assistance.
Ayar Uchu.source: Betanzos, Suma y narración de los incas

Aysavillca.myth: Seven huacas confronted by Pachacuti Inca
Aysavillca.note: Huallallo and Aysavillca jointly appear among seven curaca-like huacas subordinated by Pachacuti Inca.

Cahuillaca’s child.note: The child reveals Cuniraya as its father by crawling to him.

Caqui.note: Huallallo deploys the tropical bird against Pariacaca, who breaks its wing and petrifies it.

Catachillay.note: Catachillay and her young appear near Urcuchillay as associated celestial llamas.
Cobo says Catachillay and her young proceeded from Urcuchillay, perhaps by descent or emanation.

Cautaguan.note: Cautaguan is Catequil’s mother and produces the egg from which he emerges.
Catequil restores his dead mother to life.

Chancharuna.note: Chancharuna is named among Pariacaca's children.

Chaupi Churin Illapa.note: Middle-son Illapa is one member of Guaman Poma’s threefold thunder complex.

Chaupiñamca.note: Chaupiñamca is treated as Pariacaca's sister in Huarochirí tradition.
A secondary marginal equation with Manañamca retrospectively makes Chaupiñamca Huallallo's female counterpart.
Some passages make Pariacaca and Chaupiñamca siblings through the Sun and Hanan Maclla.
Pariacaca animates men while Chaupiñamca animates women; their festivals form a paired ritual order.

Chimbo Urma.note: Guamán Poma uniquely names Chimbo Urma among Mama Huaco's children.

Chinchacocha.myth: Seven huacas confronted by Pachacuti Inca
Chinchacocha.note: Huallallo and Chinchacocha jointly appear among seven curaca-like huacas subordinated by Pachacuti Inca.

Choquechinchay.note: Choquechinchay occupies Chasca’s counterpart position, possibly representing evening Venus.
Choquechinchay.source: Santa Cruz Pachacuti, Relación de antigüedades

Christ.note: Christ and Pachamama are invoked within the same syncretistic ritual world.

Christian God.note: Missionaries and Christian Andean authors equate or subordinate Viracocha to the Christian creator.

Christian saints.note: Saints and Christian invocations protect mines or restrain Supay-like subterranean danger.

Chucpaico.note: Chucpaico is named among Pariacaca's children.

Chuqui Ylla.note: Chasca and Chuqui Ylla share a temple cult and service by selected women.
A disputed Sun–Moon genealogy makes Chuqui Ylla Chasca’s sibling.
Modern scholarship reconstructs them as morning and evening Venus counterparts.

Chuquihuacra.myth: Seven huacas confronted by Pachacuti Inca
Chuquihuacra.note: Huallallo and Chuquihuacra jointly appear among seven curaca-like huacas subordinated by Pachacuti Inca.

Chuquihuampo.note: Chuquihuampo is named as a son of Pariacaca.
Chuquihuampo fights beside Pariacaca and is wounded in the foot by Manañamca.

Chuquisuso.note: After negotiating irrigation benefits for her community, Chuquisuso accepts union with Pariacaca.
Pariacaca supplies water and canal works after Chuquisuso negotiates lasting irrigation for her community.

Churapa.note: Churapa enters Mullucocha and turns it into a lake during Huallallo's pursuit.
Churapa is one of Pariacaca's five brothers or manifestations.
Churapa emerges and fights Huallallo jointly with Pariacaca and the other brothers.

Cocamama.note: This coca power participates with Pachamama in the agricultural generative field.

Creator.myth: Offerings travel by river through Mamacocha to the Creator
Creator.note: River-borne sacrifices could reach the Creator through or within Mamacocha.
Creator.source: Molina, Relación de las fábulas y ritos

Cuniraya Viracocha.note: Modern scholars sometimes identify coastal Con with Cuniraya, though no early source equates them.

El Tío.note: Mining ritual portrays the phallic Tío fertilizing Pachamama so she yields metal.
Bolivian miners sometimes identify Supay with the subterranean owner of ore and wealth.

First daughter of Urpayhuachac.myth: Assault and transformation into a dove
First daughter of Urpayhuachac.note: Cuniraya attempts to rape her, but she escapes by becoming a dove.

Guachemines.note: Catequil attacks the primordial Guachemines with slings, killing or expelling them.

Hanan Maclla.note: One genealogical arrangement names Hanan Maclla as Pariacaca's mother.

Huamancántac.myth: Sequential Huacho shoreline and guano-island rites
Huamancántac.note: Travelers offered chicha beside the sea, then worshipped Huamancántac on the islands.

Huamansuri.note: Huamansuri is Catequil’s father, killed before the twins emerge.
Catequil inherits the two slings Huamansuri left for his avenger.

Huanacauri.note: Uchu fastens to the pre-existing wak’a, becomes stone, and converges with Huanacauri.
Huanacauri.source: Sarmiento, Historia de los Incas, ch. 12

Huanacauri.note: Huanacauri and Chasca appear in the same sacred festival enumeration.

Huanacauri.myth: Manco petitions the brother-huaca before founding Cusco
Huanacauri.note: Manco prays to Huanacauri for favor and reveres him as a god.
Huanacauri.source: Cieza, El señorío de los incas

Huari.note: Some Oruro variants connect the underground Huari with the Devil or Supay.

Huariruma.note: Huariruma is named among Pariacaca's children.

Huatiacuri.note: Huatiacuri is paradoxically called Pariacaca's son although he precedes Pariacaca's emergence.
Pariacaca's supernatural power helps Huatiacuri expose Tantañamca and defeat his wealthy rival.

Huayllama.note: Huayllama is implicated in the expansion of Pariacaca's cult and territorial order.

Huaytapallana.note: A humanlike Amaru falls in love with Huaytapallana.
Modern Mantaro traditions identify Huallallo with the sacred snow massif and its resident apu.

Hugi.note: Huallallo produces the unidentified animal to harm Pariacaca; a Checa man eventually captures it.

Imaymana Viracochan.note: Molina describes Imaymana as Viracocha's son or emanated agent.
Viracocha sends Imaymana along the mountain or eastern route.

Inca Yupanqui.note: Guamán Poma uniquely names Inca Yupanqui among Mama Huaco's children.

Kuru.note: In an unsupported modern tale, the maiden Sara rejects the sorcerer Kuru.

Libiac.note: Writers compare this central-highland thunder power with Illapa, without a meeting myth.

Llacsa Churapa.note: Llacsa Churapa dams Pariacaca's waters, forming the lake that nearly submerges Huallallo.

Llocllayhuancupa.note: Catequil enables the previously mute wak’a to speak and reveal its mission.

Líbiac.note: Zaramama stalks and joined ears were danced with, then burned for Líbiac.
Líbiac.source: Arriaga, Extirpación de la idolatría del Pirú

Macahuisa.note: Macahuisa is described as Pariacaca's son or emanated martial agent.
Pariacaca's martial agent defeats imperial enemies using rain, lightning, and flood.
Macahuisa is named as Pariacaca's son.
Pariacaca sends Macahuisa, who defeats the Inca's rebels through catastrophic weather.

Mama Cura.note: Mama Cura is Mama Huaco's sister and fellow female Ayar founder.
Mama Cura is a fellow female member of the primordial sibling collective.
They join the same migration; no one-to-one interaction is preserved.

Mama Ipacura.note: Mama Ipacura belongs to the eightfold sibling founding group.
Mama Ipacura is paired with Ayar Uchu in Sarmiento’s allocation.

Mama Rahua.note: Mama Rahua is Mama Huaco's sister and fellow female Ayar founder.

Mama Raua.note: Mama Raua belongs to the eightfold sibling founding group.
Mama Raua is paired with Ayar Auca in Sarmiento’s allocation.
Mama Raua is a fellow female member of the primordial sibling collective.
They join the same migration; no one-to-one interaction is preserved.

Manañamca.myth: Pariacaca's campaign against the fiery beings
Manañamca.note: The fiery female supay is described as being with Huallallo, but their precise relationship is unstated.
Manañamca wounds Pariacaca's son Chuquihuampo during the combat cycle.

Menes.myth: Theosophists compare legendary founders across civilizations
Menes.note: Later Theosophical writing compares Manco with Menes as a primordial founder.

Other assembled huacas.note: Cuniraya sits among the assembled huacas disguised as a despised beggar.

Other summoned huacas.note: Pariacaca asks the assembled huacas who will help the Inca; they hesitate before Macahuisa volunteers.

Our Lady of Peace.myth: Post-siege founding of the January Alasita fair
Our Lady of Peace.note: Later legend links Ekeko’s fair to January 24, the Virgin’s feast.

Pachacamac’s elder daughter.note: She is Pachacamac and Urpayhuachac’s elder daughter.

Pachacamac’s younger daughter.note: She is Pachacamac and Urpayhuachac’s younger daughter.

Pachacuti Inca.note: Guamán Poma uniquely names Pachacuti Inca among Mama Huaco's children.

Pachamama Achi.note: Apo Manco Cápac is named as her child; identification with Pachamama is uncertain.
Pachamama Achi.source: Santa Cruz Pachacuti, Relación de antigüedades

Paria Carco.note: Paria Carco pursues Huallallo and remains a snowy sentinel preventing his return.

Pariacaca’s four brothers.note: The four brothers accompanying Pariacaca are collectively and uncertainly called Cuniraya’s sons.

Pariacarco.note: Pariacarco is one of Pariacaca's five brothers or manifestations.
Pariacarco remains toward the Antis to guard against Huallallo's return.

Piguerao.note: Piguerao is Catequil’s twin brother, emerging from the second egg.

Pleiades.note: The Pleiades appear with Inti in temple and cosmographic arrangements.

Punchao.note: Chuqui Ylla Yllapa is carried and offered to alongside Punchao.
Imperial solar worship was installed above Pachacamac’s sanctuary, expressing political hierarchy and complementarity.

Puncho.note: Puncho is named among the Pariacaca brothers collectively engaged in Huallallo's defeat.
Puncho is one of Pariacaca's five brothers or manifestations.
Puncho emerges and fights Huallallo jointly with Pariacaca and the other brothers.

Qullqipunku.note: Ausangate and Qullqipunku frame a shared pilgrimage landscape of glacier, water, and livestock fertility.

Rainbow.note: A rainbow appears as a favorable summit sign; its independent personhood is ambiguous.
Rainbow.source: Sarmiento, Historia de los Incas, ch. 12

Santiago.note: Santiago absorbed thunder and martial attributes resembling Catequil in colonial and later religion.

Santiago Apostle.note: Santiago became Illapa’s Christian successor, analogue, mask, and transformed continuation.

Saqra.note: Regional usage sometimes substitutes Saqra for Supay, although early lexicography distinguishes them.

Saramama.note: This maize power participates with Pachamama in the agricultural generative field.

Sasenmale.note: Sasenmale is named among Pariacaca's children.

Second daughter of Urpayhuachac.note: Cuniraya has intercourse with or assaults her; translations differ regarding coercion.

Señor de los Milagros.note: Rostworowski proposed a transformation linking both earthquake-associated sacred figures, without demonstrating continuous identity.

Sinchi Roca.note: Manco Cápac and Mama Ocllo procreate Sinchi Roca.
Mama Ocllo is his mother; he succeeds Manco Cápac.
Sinchi Roca is usually Manco's son and dynastic successor.

Sons of Catequil.note: Lightning stones and subsidiary wak’as are described as Catequil’s children.

Stars.myth: Creation of celestial light at Tiwanaku
Stars.note: Viracocha creates and orders the stars at Tiwanaku.
Stars.source: Betanzos, Suma y narración de los Incas

Sullca Churin Illapa.note: Younger-son Illapa is one member of Guaman Poma’s threefold thunder complex.

Sullca Illapa.note: A textually unstable or canceled reading possibly names Sullca Illapa as the fifth brother.

Sullca Yllapa.note: Sullca Yllapa appears in the uncertain list of Pariacaca persons involved in the campaign.

Taguapaca.note: After Taguapaca disobeys, Viracocha has him bound and cast onto water.
Taguapaca.source: Betanzos, Suma y narración de los Incas

Tambotoco.note: Tambotoco and Chasca appear together among Inca sacred beings and places.

Tantañamca.note: Pariacaca's son Huatiacuri exposes Tantañamca and redirects his household toward Pariacaca.

Tauris.note: Mama Sara ears were carried before Tauris, danced with, brewed, and burned.

Tayta Shanti.note: Living Mantaro practice situationally identifies the Huaytapallana mountain being with Tayta Shanti.

Titicaca.note: Titicaca and Chasca occur in the same sacred enumeration.

Tiw.myth: Transformation of Tiw into the Diablada devil
Tiw.note: Oruro heritage narratives connect Tiw with the festival figure later called Devil or Supay.

Tocapo Viracochan.note: Molina describes Tocapo as Viracocha's second son or emanated agent.

Tocapo Viracochan.myth: Ordering peoples along the second route
Tocapo Viracochan.note: Viracocha sends Tocapo along another route to continue ordering creation.

Tulumanya.note: The rainbow power Tulumanya engenders Amaru in modern folklore versions.

Tunupa.note: Bertonio equates Ecaco with Thunnupa, indicating identity or close local equivalence.
Tunupa.source: Bertonio, Vocabulario de la lengua aymara

Tunupa.note: Tunupa expels Uallollo and other huacas to the snowy mountains.
Writers compare this southern storm and culture-hero power with Illapa.
Some writers equate Tunupa with Taguapaca or a Viracocha-like wandering preacher.
Tunupa.source: Santa Cruz Pachacuti and later scholarship

Tutayquiri.note: Tutayquiri is Pariacaca's conquering son, whose advance into Yunca territory Chuquisuso halts.

Tutañamca.note: Huallallo defeats Tutañamca alongside Yanañamca and assumes sovereignty.

Túpac Inca Yupanqui.note: Pariacaca answers the sacred Inca's request by sending Macahuisa against the rebels.

Unnamed child of Cahuillaca.note: Cuniraya fathers Cahuillaca’s unnamed child, who recognizes him before becoming stone offshore.

Unnamed heavenly maiden.note: A brother plausibly identified with Illapa breaks her jar, producing storms and rain.

Urpayhuachac.note: While seeking Cavillaca, Cuniraya retaliates against Urpayhuachac's fish-related order.
Cuniraya takes Urpayhuachac's captive fish and throws them into the ocean, where they multiply.
Urpayhuachac pursues Cuniraya and plots to crush him with a rock, but he escapes.
Cuniraya takes fish from Urpayhuachac’s pond and casts them into the ocean.
Urpayhuachac tries to lure Cuniraya into a trap or precipice, but he escapes.
Urpayhuachac is Pachacamac’s wife and head of his coastal household.
Cuniraya retaliates against absent Urpayhuachac by casting her fish into the sea.

Urpayhuachac’s daughters.note: Cuniraya attempts sexual aggression against Urpayhuachac's daughters; one escapes.

Utcochuco.note: Utcochuco is named among Pariacaca's children.

Uñachillay.myth: The neighboring celestial llama and calf
Uñachillay.note: Lehmann-Nitsche conjecturally restored this name for the young llama appearing near Urcuchillay.

Vichama.note: Inti engenders or creates Vichama after Pachacamac murders the first child.
Inti hears or assists Vichama following Pachacamac's violence.

Vichama.myth: The Sun sends three social eggs
Vichama.note: Inti sends three eggs from which ranked human groups emerge.
Calancha describes Pachacamac and Vichama as brothers within the story’s logic.
Vichama seeks vengeance for his mother’s murder; Pachacamac escapes into the sea.

Virgin Mary.note: Some worshippers identify or analogize Mary and Pachamama through maternal and landscape devotion.

Virgin of the Socavón.note: Festival devils identified loosely with Supay dance devotionally before the Virgin and submit to Marian order.

Yacana.note: Modern comparisons sometimes equate them, but the sources preserve distinct names and celestial forms.

Yana Raman.note: Writers classify this Yaro or Llacuaz thunder being as an Illapa counterpart.

Yanañamca.note: Huallallo defeats Yanañamca and succeeds to the rule of the land.

Yayan Illapa.note: Father Illapa is the senior member of Guaman Poma’s threefold thunder complex.

dead mitayos.note: One mining narrative says dead colonial laborers became Tíos or joined the subterranean master.

first race of giants.note: Viracocha creates a primordial race of giants before making the second humanity.
Viracocha destroys the disobedient giants by flood or petrification.

saints.note: Saints and Pachamama are invoked within the same ritual world without necessary identification.

the Christian God.note: Colonial authors equated Pachacamac’s invisible creator role with the Christian God.

the Lord of Qoyllur Rit’i.note: Ausangate's mountain landscape is ritually related to the Christian image and sanctuary.

the rainbow.note: The rainbow appears with Inti in temple and cosmographic arrangements.

the stars.note: The stars appear with Inti in temple and cosmographic arrangements.
The Moon and stars jointly rose from Titicaca into the sky.

two Cañari huacas.myth: Seven huacas confronted by Pachacuti Inca
two Cañari huacas.note: Two unnamed Cañari huacas appear with Huallallo among the seven beings subordinated by Pachacuti Inca.
